Research sprint · 27 Aug 2026 · reviewing the composed suite

The Carry

A component & motion playbook for Signal Studio

The redesign already solved the hard problem: three products on one floor, all mounted at once, none ever torn down. What is left is one missing frame of continuity, and a token vocabulary with three names for the same speed.

3→1products now share one floor, one spine, one sheet
4names between them for three speeds
~5lines to turn the switch into a carry
477raw <button> elements, no Button primitive

01The redesign got the hard part right

Captured from the composed suite's own source at 1440×900, at ?p=tasks, ?p=notes and ?p=timeline.

This is settled, and it was the largest open question in the suite. One ink floor, one floating spine, one white sheet, one rail language, one primary-button language. An earlier draft of this playbook audited the shipping app and reported three different chromes and three different primary buttons; the composed suite fixed both. That finding is withdrawn.

The part that matters most is architectural, not visual

app.js mounts all three products at once and never tears one down:

/* Nothing is torn down. The product leaving keeps its DOM, its scroll,
   its focus and every fact it was holding… Sort the board, read a note,
   come back — the board is still sorted. */

That is the substrate “the interface transforms rather than replaces” requires, and it is already built. Most products that want this effect have to rebuild their routing to get it.

Also right, and worth protecting

  • The lane subtitles are the best writing in the product. “Held by a reply, a delivery, or a decision.” under WAITING. This explains a kanban board to someone who has never used one — the first-contact test passed inside the interface rather than alongside it.
  • Motion is already tokenised and scoped. A moved milestone animates its position with the note that this “animates the distance rather than decorating a state change” — the thesis of §05, arrived at independently.
  • The accessibility work is above the industry norm. Hidden products are made inert; focus moves to the arriving sheet and the arrival is announced; coarse pointers get real 44px controls; the spine's focus ring is white rather than indigo because indigo measured 2.56:1 on composited ink — under the 3:1 floor.

One delivery note, separate from the design. As rendered in demo mode at a709e22: /app/tasks renders the floor; /app/notes and /app/timeline still render the previous chrome. The design work is done — landing it is not.

02The one missing frame

Everything needed for continuity is in place except the continuity itself.

// app.js — go() → apply(). Both products are in the document at this instant.
host.toggleAttribute("hidden", !on);
host.setAttribute("inert", "");
↑ nothing interpolates between them. The switch is a hard cut.

Because both DOMs coexist in one document, this is the easy form of the problem. No navigation, no @view-transition at-rule, no two-page opt-in, no same-origin question, and none of the programmatic-navigation exclusion that would have blocked the old architecture:

function apply() {
  if (!document.startViewTransition || reducedMotion) return applyNow();
  document.startViewTransition(applyNow);
}

Plus view-transition-name on the sheet and on the active rail tile. Roughly five lines against an architecture that was built to receive them.

The previous suite navigated with window.location.href after a deliberate 120 ms delay, which structurally disqualified it from the platform's own transition. The redesign deleted that problem wholesale. What remains is not a defect so much as an unfinished sentence.

Built, not just proposed

This is not a recommendation on paper. The change above was applied to a duplicate of the composed suite and it works — one startViewTransition call per switch, two names, no errors, and the departing product's scroll, focus and state survive the transition intact.

One refinement the prototype needed, found by looking at it rather than by reasoning about it: the browser's default cross-fade runs both snapshots at 50% through the middle, and two dense text layouts at half opacity read as mud, not as a change. A fade-through fixes it — outgoing gone by 40%, incoming from 40% on, so they never overlap:

::view-transition-old(sheet) { animation: carry-out  88ms cubic-bezier(.4,0,1,1) both; }
::view-transition-new(sheet) { animation: carry-in  132ms cubic-bezier(0,0,.2,1) 88ms both; }

The sheet and the rail tile still carry for the full 220ms underneath. What fades is only the part that genuinely is new.

03Three speeds, four names

The composed suite's declared ladder is three tight steps and one default curve. That is a good ladder. The drift is not in the values — it is in the names.

ValueNames it answers toTransition uses
140ms--dur · --t-base · --motion-fast46 · 5 · 1
220ms--dur-settle · --t-slow · --motion-base5 · 2 · 1
cubic-bezier(.23,1,.32,1)--ease · --curve · --ease-out— · 3 · —
50ms--dur-outdeclared, never used

Two reviewers cannot tell whether two components move identically without resolving the aliases first. And the --t- prefix is overloaded across dimensions: --t-base is 0.14s while --t-11 … --t-34 are type sizes in pixels. The prefix means both time and type.

And there is no rare tier. --motion-slow: 400ms is declared and used in zero transitions — in practice nothing moves for longer than 220ms. Correct for the frequent and occasional tiers, and it leaves the suite with no vocabulary at all for a moment that has earned one.

04Five directions, two rejected

Explored as competing directions and scored honestly. The most visually exciting one is rejected; the one that wins is the one that makes the product easier to use.

Direction A

Fluid / gooey / morphing

The intent — identity survives the change — is the most valuable idea in the brief. The technique usually meant by it is an SVG filter stack that re-rasterises every frame, destroys subpixel text rendering, and is the most datable idiom in this list.

Intent only
Direction B

Spring / physical / tactile

Springs interrupt gracefully — a retargeted spring carries its velocity where a tween restarts and stutters. But bounce is the fastest way to make a professional tool feel like a toy. Adopt the physics, budget the bounce.

Adopt · bounded
Direction C

Spatial / shared-element

The only direction that answers the brief's actual question, now a platform feature rather than a library trick. Uniquely, it reduces bespoke animation code — the browser interpolates. And it makes the product easier to use: when the object you clicked is visibly the object that opened, you never lose your place.

Adopt · the spine
Direction D

Liquid Glass / material

Wrong material for a product whose metaphor is paper on ink. Translucency over white paper produces grey. It makes text contrast a function of whatever scrolls beneath — unverifiable by the contrast gate this repo actually enforces — and backdrop-filter is the most expensive common effect on the web.

Reject
Direction E

Signal / technical / precision

The direction most already true of this product — tabular numerics, hairlines, lane counts, the “79 days” counter. Adopting it formally costs almost nothing. Taken too far it becomes cold, and these users are planning weddings: precision in timing and geometry, warmth in language.

Adopt · the tone

05The carry

The suite's vocabulary is already physical and concrete: the floor, the spine, the sheet. The motion language extends it rather than importing a new one.

Things in Signal Studio are carried from one place to the next. They are never destroyed and rebuilt.

That sentence produces a falsifiable test for every proposed animation: is something being carried, or is something being performed? If nothing is being carried, the animation is decoration and should be cut.

01
Nothing that survives a change may be redrawn.If an object exists before an interaction and after it, it must be the same object on screen, moved. The card that opens the panel is the panel's header.
02
The object leads; the container follows.Transitions anchor to what the user touched, not to the viewport. Nothing slides in from a screen edge unless the gesture came from that edge.
03
Frequency sets amplitude.The more often an interaction happens, the less it may move. A hard budget with numbers, not a sensibility.
04
Motion may never be the reason to wait.No animation on the critical path. Optimistic update, then animate the result. This law alone deletes suiteJump's 120ms.

The frequency budget — Law 3, with numbers

TierExamplesMax durationMax translateBounce
Frequent
many per minute		hover, press, focus, tab, checkbox80ms0px0
Occasional
several per hour		open task, open menu, switch view, move card220ms8px≤0.15
Rare
a few per day or less		clear a lane, finish onboarding, publish a timeline480ms16px≤0.35

The frequent tier permitting zero translation is deliberate and is the most important row in this document. Hover states that move are the most common way a professional tool becomes tiring.

Springs — duration and bounce, not stiffness and damping

Following Apple's Spring(duration:bounce:) and Motion v12's visualDuration + bounce — already a dependency, so no new library is required for anything in this playbook.

TokenvisualDurationbounceUse
SPRING_CRISP0.140Press, toggle, checkbox — anything frequent
SPRING_CARRY0.220.12Card→panel, lane reflow, drag settle
SPRING_ARRIVE0.320.24Something new appearing
SPRING_REWARD0.480.35Celebration only. Rare by definition

Bounce above 0.35 is not available. Nothing in a wedding-coordination tool needs it.

The top of the list is dominated by coherence and enforcement, not animation. The two most visually exciting items sit mid-table because they are expensive. Nine of the fifteen Monday items contain little or no animation. Two are deletions.

07Monday — start here

The first six, in order. Items 1–4 are a two-day pair-programmable block. Acceptance criteria are written to be failed.

01

Delete suiteJump, opt into cross-document view transitions

Complexity SNet deletionglobals.css · suite-switcher-pills · suite-launcher

Current — onClick calls preventDefault() on a real anchor, paints a 260ms curtain, sets location.href after a deliberate 120ms timeout.

Desired — the pill is an ordinary link. The browser performs the transition. The sheet persists; the spine's active tile carries to its new position.

Acceptance
  • A product switch performs no setTimeout and creates no overlay element.
  • The sheet does not blink: continuously present across the navigation, its radius and inset unchanged during it.
  • The active tile travels to its new position — not one tile extinguishing and another lighting.
  • Under reduced motion, navigation still occurs and is instant.
  • Without browser support, behaviour is exactly today's — verified, not assumed.
02

Give Notes and Timeline the Tasks chrome

Complexity MMostly CSSBlocks item 01's payoff

Current — three products, three chromes (§01). Desired — one floor, one spine, one sheet. The composition lock already decides every disputed value.

Acceptance
  • Screenshots of all three at 1440 are indistinguishable in chrome: same rail width, inset, sheet radius, wordmark position.
  • The primary action in all three is the same component with the same variant — Timeline's indigo pill and Notes' outline button both resolve to Button variants.
  • No product declares --paper at :root.
  • The three-product screenshot strip is regenerated and attached to the PR.
03

Button and IconButton

Complexity ML to migrate fullyDo not attempt all 477 this week

Current — 477 raw buttons, at least four primary designs, inconsistent disabled treatment. Desired — one component, four variants, one press behaviour, one focus ring.

Acceptance
  • Press is SPRING_CRISP (0.14 / bounce 0) and does not translate.
  • Loading swaps the label in place and preserves width — no reflow.
  • Disabled is cursor: default and non-focusable, matching the rule the Tasks lab already states.
  • No variant accepts a className that changes colour, radius or spacing.
04

check-motion-contract.mjs, in report mode

Complexity SMirror the existing ratchet script

Fail on duration literals that aren't var(--motion-*), and on cubic-bezier outside globals.css. Honour /* ds-allow — reason */ and require the reason. Baseline at today's numbers so the sprint burns them down instead of blocking on day one.

Acceptance
  • Reports exactly 32 durations and 16 curves on the current tree — different numbers mean it is measuring the wrong thing.
  • A new off-contract duration raises the count and fails the ratchet.
  • A ds-allow without a reason fails.
05

Calendar: role="grid", roving tabindex, arrow keys

Complexity S–MCorrectness only — no motion in this item

Current — due-calendar.tsx has no grid role, no onKeyDown, and 42 sequential tab stops. Animating a control a keyboard user cannot operate is the wrong order.

Acceptance
  • Tab enters the grid once and lands on the selected day, or today.
  • Every day reachable by arrows; PageUp/Down by month; Home/End by week.
  • Changing month by keyboard moves focus to the equivalent day.
  • axe reports zero violations on the open picker.
06

Card → panel shared element

Complexity MLaw 1, in its most-used form

The card the user clicked becomes the panel header, so they never lose their place on the board.

Acceptance
  • The clicked card's title is continuously on screen throughout — never cross-faded or re-rendered in place.
  • Closing returns to the same card, in the same lane, at the same scroll position.
  • Opening a second task from within the panel carries again, with no flash to the board between.
  • ≤220ms, --ease-standard.

Items 07–15 — curve retirement, Popover and Tooltip, date-picker motion, in-product view transitions, AI staggered arrival, toast anchoring, the last six reduced-motion blocks, board drag transport, and Note→Task carry — are specified in full in the committed playbook at docs/COMPONENT_AND_MOTION_PLAYBOOK.md.

The brief's closing principle is the right one. This playbook's only substantive amendment is a matter of sequence: the goal is not more animation — the goal is that every interaction feels considered. Considered first requires consistent. That is week one.
